analysis.one_liner: Extends several specific drug and food-ingredient patents, including Procter & Gamble's olestra fat substitute.
analysis.headline: A private bill extending exclusive rights to several patents — including olestra, a Procter & Gamble fat substitute — passed the Senate by voice vote on October 8, 1992, but died in the House without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This was private legislation: instead of changing the law for everyone, it singled out specific patents. It would have extended Procter & Gamble's olestra fat-substitute patents through the end of 1997, extended an Ethiofos drug patent by three years and a painkiller patent by two, and renewed design patents on the American Legion and United Daughters of the Confederacy insignias. It also set out stricter standards that Congress says future patent-extension bills should have to meet. The Senate passed it on a voice vote, but the House never acted before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The holders of the named patents. Procter & Gamble would keep exclusive control of olestra through 1997, blocking anyone else from making the fat substitute during that window. The Ethiofos patent holder would get three more years of exclusive rights, and the painkiller patent holder two more years, both beyond the normal patent term. The American Legion and United Daughters of the Confederacy would regain exclusive control of their insignia designs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Named patent holders, mainly Procter & Gamble

how_it_helps.text: Extends the three olestra patents (4,005,195, 4,005,196, and 4,034,083) through December 31, 1997, keeping exclusive rights with their owner past the normal expiration dates.

Extends the Ethiofos patent (3,892,824) for three years when it expires, and extends a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug patent (3,793,457) for two years, limited to uses already approved by the FDA.

Renews design patents for the American Legion, its Women's Auxiliary, the Sons of the American Legion, and the United Daughters of the Confederacy for 14 years, while protecting anyone who began using the designs after the originals expired.

Requires that, before certifying the olestra extension, the patent owner must submit an FDA-agreed post-market surveillance program tracking how olestra affects people's fat intake, with the data made available to Congress for public review.

States that Congress should not approve future patent-extension bills unless the patent holder shows government misconduct or a serious government-caused injury, and that harm to the public (such as through higher prices) must be outweighed.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and would-be competitors. Every extra year of an extended patent is an extra year without competition, which the bill's own standards section acknowledges means higher prices for the public. Companies hoping to enter the fat-substitute and drug markets would stay shut out during the extension windows.

drawbacks.text: The extensions give named companies years of additional exclusive rights past the normal patent term, and the bill itself concedes that extension causes 'harm to the public (such as through higher prices)' — the extensions were granted anyway.

Granting extensions one patent at a time through private bills sidesteps the standard patent term that applies to everyone else, and the stricter standards in Section 2 are phrased as findings about what Congress 'should' do in the future — they are non-binding and do not govern the extensions this bill itself grants.

The olestra extension came with only a self-reported surveillance requirement: the company requests certification and attaches a statement that it and the FDA agreed on a study, leaving the continued monopoly as the default.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains flow almost entirely to a handful of patent holders — chiefly Procter & Gamble's multi-year lock on olestra — while the costs fall diffusely on consumers through longer monopoly pricing and on excluded competitors. The one public-facing feature, a stricter set of standards for future patent-extension bills, is non-binding and was packaged alongside new special extensions, so it does not offset the transfers. This is a narrowly drawn favor to specific rights holders, and it died before taking effect.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the Senate by voice vote in October 1992, but the House Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator John Glenn on July 19, 1991 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the introduced version would have extended one patent for ten years.

The Senate Judiciary subcommittee held hearings on August 1, 1991, approved a substitute version in May 1992, and the full committee reported it favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on September 22, 1992.
The Senate passed the amended bill by voice vote on October 8, 1992; a voice vote means no individual votes are recorded.
The House received the bill on October 9, 1992 and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and would-be competitors came out ahead: the olestra fat-substitute and drug monopolies expired on their normal schedules, and Procter & Gamble and the other patent holders did not get the extra exclusive years they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and competitors; patent holders lost

for.name: Sen. John Glenn
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the patent-extension bill and carried it through Senate committee and floor passage.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, approved a substitute version, and reported the bill favorably to the Senate floor in September 1992.

for.name: The Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the amended bill by voice vote on October 8, 1992, sending it to the House with no recorded votes.

for.name: Procter & Gamble
for.what_they_did: Sought extension of its olestra patents; the bill was drafted around its fat-substitute patents and Senate hearings covered the product's regulatory delays.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee where the bill sat after Senate passage
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 9, 1992 and took no further action; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed it by voice vote, so no individual votes exist; its four cosponsors split 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat, and the bill died in House committee without a vote, leaving no record of party positions.

industries.note: The bill would have kept P&G's exclusive rights to olestra through December 31, 1997, past the patents' normal expiration. A longer monopoly delays competing fat substitutes and keeps prices up for snack-food makers and the consumers who buy from them; the bill's own standards section names higher prices as public harm from extensions.

industries.industry: Drug patent holders (Ethiofos and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory)
industries.note: Three extra years on the Ethiofos patent and two on the painkiller patent, beyond normal terms, mean extended exclusive pricing on those drugs. The painkiller extension was limited to already-FDA-approved uses.

industries.industry: Veterans and civic organizations (American Legion, United Daughters of the Confederacy)
industries.note: Renews 14-year exclusive rights to their insignia design patents, with protection for people who began using the designs after the originals expired. The effect on the public is negligible.
